t: Dice Roll Simulation — Counting Constrained Sequences with DP
o: We must count length-$n$ sequences over faces 1..6 where no face $i$ appears more than `rollMax[i-1]` times **consecutively**. The only state that matters beyond the roll index is *which face was just rolled* and *how many consecutive times it has been rolled so far* — because the constraint is purely about consecutive runs. In Example 1 ($n=2$), all 36 pairs are valid except (1,1) and (2,2), giving 34. Example 3 shows the count grows fast, so brute-force enumeration of $6^n$ sequences (up to $6^{5000}$) is impossible; we need to share subproblems. Since $n \le 5000$ and each face can run at most 15 times, a DP over states $(\text{roll}, \text{face}, \text{run length})$ — at most $5000 \times 6 \times 15 = 450{,}000$ states — is easily feasible.
k: The constraint only involves consecutive runs, so tracking (current face, current run length) is sufficient state.
A transition either extends the current run (if run length < rollMax[face]) or switches to any other face starting a run of length 1.
Answer = sum over all ending states after n rolls; work modulo 1e9+7.

a.i: Define dfs(rollsLeft, face, run) = number of ways to finish the remaining rolls given that face was just rolled `run` consecutive times. From this state we try every next face f: if f == face we may continue only when run < rollMax[face], otherwise we start a fresh run of 1. Memoizing on (rollsLeft, face, run) collapses the exponential recursion tree to O(n·6·15) distinct states.
s: For each candidate face f in 0..5: if f == face require run < rollMax[face], new run = run+1; else new run = 1.
Start by iterating over the first roll's face with run = 1 and summing dfs(n-1, f, 1).
a.t: O(n · 6 · 15 · 6) time — each of the ~450k memoized states loops over 6 faces.
a.sp: O(n · 6 · 15) for the memo table plus recursion stack up to depth n.

a.i: Flip the recursion into iteration. Let dp[f][r] be the number of valid sequences of the rolls processed so far that end with face f repeated exactly r times. Initially dp[f][1] = 1. For each new roll, extending face f gives dp'[f][r+1] += dp[f][r] when r < rollMax[f]; switching from g ≠ f gives dp'[f][1] += dp[g][r]. The answer is the sum of all dp values after n rolls. This avoids recursion overhead and can use rolling arrays.
s: Initialize dp[f][1] = 1 for all six faces (one roll used).
For each of the remaining n-1 rolls, build a fresh ndp table.
Extension: for each face f and run r < rollMax[f], ndp[f][r+1] += dp[f][r].
Switch: for each face f, ndp[f][1] += sum of dp[g][r] over all g != f and all valid r.
Return the sum of all dp entries modulo 1e9+7.
a.t: O(n · 6 · 15 · 6) ≈ O(n) — constant factors are tiny since 6 and 15 are fixed bounds.
a.sp: O(6 · 15) using two rolling DP tables.

w: In an interview, start with the memoized recursion to demonstrate the state design (roll index, last face, run length), then present the bottom-up version as the clean optimal solution. Common pitfalls: forgetting that switching faces resets the run to 1, off-by-one errors on whether run counts include the current roll, and missing the modulo on intermediate sums (use 64-bit accumulators in C++/Java). Edge cases: n = 1 always returns 6 regardless of rollMax; rollMax[i] = 1 forbids immediate repeats of face i. Follow-ups might ask for an O(n·6) solution using prefix sums per face, or handling a variable number of faces k.
